title: Cost of debt and capital structure

objectives: Answer out loud: How do you find cost of debt?
Answer out loud: Why not use unlimited debt?

steps.body: Cost of debt = yield to maturity on the company's existing debt (what the market demands today) — not the coupon.
If no traded debt: use the credit rating's typical spread over the risk-free rate (a synthetic rating from interest coverage).
Multiply by (1 − t) for the after-tax cost.

blocks.title: Why is debt cheaper than equity?
blocks.teaser: Debt holders get paid first (contractual interest, priority in bankruptcy), so they bear less risk and accept a lower return.
blocks.body:
Debt holders get paid first (contractual interest, priority in bankruptcy), so they bear less risk and accept a lower return. Interest is also tax-deductible.

**Interview answer:** "Debt is senior and contractual, so it's less risky, and interest is tax-deductible."

blocks.title: Why YTM and not the coupon?
blocks.teaser: The coupon was set when the bond was issued.
blocks.body: The coupon was set when the bond was issued. YTM reflects what investors require today, which is what a new investor would demand.

blocks.title: If debt is cheaper, should a company use as much as possible?
blocks.body:
No. WACC follows a U-shape. Adding some debt lowers WACC (cheap, tax-deductible capital). But as debt rises, bankruptcy risk rises, so both the cost of equity and cost of debt rise. Past a point, WACC increases.

**Interview answer:** "Up to a point. More debt raises the risk for everyone, so the cost of debt and equity both rise, and eventually WACC goes back up."

blocks.prompt: Debt is cheaper than equity. Does adding more debt always lower WACC?

options.text: Yes — cheaper capital always lowers the average
No — past a point, distress risk raises both the cost of debt and equity, so WACC rises
Yes, as long as interest is tax-deductible

blocks.explanation: WACC is U-shaped: some debt lowers it, but too much raises bankruptcy risk and pushes up the cost of both debt and equity.

blocks.title: What if the company has no taxable income?
blocks.teaser: It can't use the interest tax shield, so the after-tax cost of debt equals the pre-tax cost.
blocks.body: It can't use the interest tax shield, so the after-tax cost of debt equals the pre-tax cost. Using (1 − t) would understate WACC.

blocks.title: Can cost of debt ever exceed cost of equity?
blocks.body: Not logically. Equity is junior and riskier, so it must require at least as much return. If your numbers show otherwise (e.g., distressed debt yields vs. a low beta), the beta is likely wrong.

blocks.title: What's Modigliani-Miller?
blocks.teaser: In a world with no taxes, bankruptcy costs, or frictions, a company's value doesn't depend on its capital structure.
blocks.body: In a world with no taxes, bankruptcy costs, or frictions, a company's value doesn't depend on its capital structure. Real-world value differences come from the things MM assumes away — mainly the tax shield (adds value) and distress costs (subtracts).
